intro_text:
Cable Beach is a 22-kilometer stretch of white sand on the eastern Indian Ocean, and also the name of the suburb around it, in the Shire of Broome, Western Australia. The beach lies about 4 km west of the Broome central business district, at roughly 17.95°S, 122.21°E on the Kimberley coast. It is one long, continuous frontage rather than a series of separate coves, and it is the reference point most visitors mean when they say they are going to Broome's beach.

Cable Beach takes its name from the telegraph cable laid between Broome and Java in 1889, part of the international submarine telegraph network of that era. The suburb around the beach had a population of 5,436 at the 2016 census, the most recent count available for the area.

The beach's most persistent subculture is not the camel trains but the naturists who have gathered since the 1960s on a stretch called "north of the rocks," north of the main car park, to sunbake, fish and swim without clothes. It is one of Australia's best-known clothes-optional beaches, but by the mid-2010s a regular there said only three or four people still came down consistently, sharing the same 100-metre run of sand with the camel tour operators leading strings of tourists past at sunrise and sunset. The fuller story of that shrinking overlap is in the culture deep-dive.

Cable Beach is not risk-free water. Box jellyfish, or stingers, may be present between November and April, and caution is advised for swimmers through that stretch of the year. The Shire of Broome and local lifeguards treat the beach's marine hazards as a standing concern rather than a hypothetical one.
spike_explainer:
Cable Beach's clothes-optional strip is the kind of local institution that survives by staying out of the brochure. Since the 1960s, naturists have gathered on the section known as "north of the rocks," north of the beach access road from the car park, to sunbake, fish and swim in the nude. Wikipedia calls it one of Australia's most famous nudist beaches, and for decades it operated on an understanding as old as the practice itself: a quiet stretch of sand, self-selecting company, and no one making a fuss about it either way.

That understanding has been getting harder to keep. The same stretch of coast that made "north of the rocks" attractive to naturists — remote, wide, unpatrolled by the standards of a city beach — is also the stretch that Broome's tourism industry built its signature product on. Camel rides are available around sunrise and sunset, the hours when the light is best and the crowds are thickest, and as of 2016 Broome's three camel tour companies operated within the same 100-metre stretch as the clothing-optional section. That is not a coincidence of geography so much as a collision of two different uses for the same narrow band of sand, one that predates the other by decades and has no formal priority over it.

The numbers tell the rest of the story. A 2016 ABC News report on the state of naturism in Australia found that the once-crowded strip had thinned out substantially: one longtime regular said plainly that only three or four people still came down on any given day. That is a steep drop from a tradition that, by its own account, once drew enough people to be considered a fixture of Broome life rather than a curiosity. The report frames the cause as generational and cultural — nudism's popularity fading nationally, not just at Cable Beach — but the camel operation detail complicates that reading. It is one thing for a practice to quietly go out of fashion. It is another for it to be sharing its remaining ground, literally every day, with a tour product built to move as many paying customers as possible past the same spot, "meaning there are hundreds more sets of peering eyes moving slowly past," in the ABC's own phrasing.

Neither side is cast as the villain in the source material, and the page will not invent one. The camel operators are running a legitimate, long-running Broome business on a public beach; nothing in the record suggests they chose their route to displace anyone. The naturists have no more formal claim to "north of the rocks" than anyone else does — there is no bylaw carving out the strip for clothes-optional use, just custom. What the record does support is the shape of the pressure: a small, aging group of regulars, holding onto a specific patch of a specific beach, watching the exact same patch absorb more foot and hoof traffic every season as Broome's tourism economy grows around it. Nothing in the sources suggests the arrangement is protected or permanent.

It is also worth being honest about what is not known. There is no post-2016 count of how many naturists still use the strip, no indication of whether the three-or-four figure has held, grown, or gone to zero in the years since, and no record of any formal move — by the Shire of Broome or anyone else — to protect or restrict the area either way. The 2025 closure of the beach's vehicle ramp for a foreshore redevelopment, and the accompanying rule that pedestrian access to "north of the rocks" and the camels now runs through the surf club gate rather than a car park at the site, changes how everyone reaches that stretch of sand, naturists included, but nothing in the source material connects that infrastructure project to the naturist story directly. It is a separate pressure on the same geography, arriving at the same time, and it is one more way the beach that once required almost no infrastructure at all is now being actively managed, gated, and rerouted around its visitors.

What makes this a genuine spike rather than a curiosity is the contrast it sits inside: Cable Beach is marketed, correctly, as a photogenic, camel-ride, sunset-postcard destination, and it is also, quietly and without much fanfare, the site of one of the country's most enduring nudist traditions — a tradition that, by its own participants' account, is now down to a handful of people sharing their strip of sand with the very tourism machine that made the beach famous in the first place.
honest_reckoning_note:
Cable Beach is marketed as a gentle, family-safe swimming beach, and most days it is exactly that. But the record does not support treating it as risk-free. Potentially deadly Irukandji jellyfish forced its closure at least twice in the years covered by this sheet: once in May 2010, after a tourist and a local resident were both stung over a single weekend, and again in September 2015, when Shire of Broome lifeguards caught a fully grown Irukandji, described by a senior lifeguard as about the size of a thumbnail, during a routine net drag. None of this makes the beach unusually dangerous by Kimberley standards, but it does mean the marketing image of calm, safe water sits alongside a documented history of venomous-jellyfish closures that the postcard version leaves out.

There is a second honest gap: Broome's lifeguards do not patrol Cable Beach at all during the tropical season, roughly late October to early April, which overlaps directly with the box jellyfish season the same tourism material warns visitors about. Patrols return only for the dry season. A beach can be genuinely worth visiting and still be a place where "safe swimming" is a seasonal, not year-round, claim.
reckoning_pullquote: Cable Beach markets a gentle family swim; the record shows two jellyfish closures and an unpatrolled season that overlaps with stinger warnings.

margin_notes.text: Cable Beach is washed by tides that can reach over nine metres, one of the larger tidal ranges on the Australian coast, which is why so much sand is exposed or submerged over the course of a single day.
The suburb sits in the state electorate of Kimberley and the federal division of Durack, postcode 6726, and contains a government primary school, Cable Beach Primary School.
Crocodiles have occasionally been sighted off Cable Beach's shore, and the Shire of Broome takes preventative measures when that happens; it is not a standing daily risk, but it is not zero, either.
Broome's beaches, Cable Beach included, are not patrolled by lifeguards during the tropical season, usually late October to early April — the same window box jellyfish warnings cover.

day_in_time.dawn: At first light the tide, which can swing over nine metres, dictates how much sand is actually there to walk on; an outgoing dawn tide can expose a very wide flat, while an incoming one narrows the beach fast.
day_in_time.midday: Midday is when the nine-metre-plus tidal range is most obvious: sandbanks that were dry an hour earlier can be underwater, and the beach's usable width changes visibly within a single visit.
day_in_time.golden: Camel rides run around sunrise and sunset hours, and the golden-hour run is the one most visitors see, the trains moving along the sand as the light drops.
day_in_time.night: After dark, a gate at the Cable Beach amphitheatre is locked whenever vehicle access is not permitted, and also during turtle nesting season, closing off the vehicle approach entirely outside patrol hours.

food_drink.name: No on-beach dining
food_drink.description: Nothing in the available sourcing names a restaurant, cafe, or kiosk on Cable Beach itself; food service, where it exists, is a matter for Broome's town centre rather than the beach frontage.
food_drink.where: Broome town centre, about 4 km from the beach

timeline.title: Telegraph cable gives the beach its name
timeline.description: A telegraph cable is laid between Broome and Java; Cable Beach is later named for it.

timeline.title: Gantheaume Point lighthouse built
timeline.description: The lighthouse at Gantheaume Point, at the southern end of Cable Beach, is built, one of ten built on the WA coast 1900-1913.
timeline.source: Heritage Council of Western Australia, via Broome Visitor Centre

timeline.title: Four beachgoers stung by jellyfish
timeline.description: Broome News reports four beachgoers stung by jellyfish at Cable Beach, treated at Broome District Hospital.

timeline.title: Irukandji jellyfish close the beach
timeline.description: Two Irukandji stings over a weekend, the fourth of the season, close Cable Beach through to Gantheaume Point; it reopens the Sunday after a clear net drag.

timeline.title: Storm damages Anastasia's Pool
timeline.description: A storm damages Anastasia's Pool, the rockpool a lighthouse keeper carved at Gantheaume Point for his arthritic wife.

timeline.title: Lifeguards catch an Irukandji, beach closes again
timeline.description: Shire of Broome lifeguards catch a fully grown Irukandji jellyfish during a routine net drag, closing Cable Beach; the last sting in Broome had been the previous April.

timeline.title: Lifeguards scheduled to return for the dry season
timeline.description: Lifeguard patrols are scheduled to return to Cable Beach on Good Friday, 3 April 2026.

zones.name: Gantheaume Point
zones.character: The extreme southern end of Cable Beach, about a 5 km walk from the main beach, with a 1905 lighthouse and dinosaur footprints visible in the rocks at low tide. A vantage point for dolphins and migrating whales, and the site of Anastasia's Pool, a rockpool damaged by a 2014 storm.
zones.best_for: Whale and dolphin watching, low-tide fossil footprints
zones.notes: Reached by the 5 km walk from Cable Beach or separately by road.

zones.name: Main beach and surf club frontage
zones.character: The patrolled swimming section in front of the Broome Surf Life Saving Club during the dry season, and the main public access point onto the 22 km beach.
zones.best_for: Patrolled swimming (dry season), general beach access
zones.notes: Access to the northern sections during Stage 2 redevelopment works runs through this point.

zones.name: North of the rocks
zones.character: The stretch north of the beach access road where four-wheel drive vehicles are permitted at low tide, and where the beach's camel tour operators run their rides.
zones.best_for: 4WD exploration at low tide, camel rides
zones.notes: Vehicle speed limit is 15 km/h; pedestrian-only access via the surf club during the 2025-2026 ramp closure.

landmarks.name: Gantheaume Point Lighthouse
landmarks.description: Built in 1905, one of ten lighthouses built on the Western Australian coast between 1900 and 1913, at the southern tip of Cable Beach. Nearby, dinosaur footprints estimated at 130 million years old by Wikipedia (120 million by the Broome Visitor Centre) are visible in the rocks at low tide.

landmarks.name: Minyirr Park
landmarks.description: A coastal reserve adjacent to the southern section of Cable Beach protecting the traditional land of the Yawuru people, with walking trails behind the red ochre dunes.

cultural_refs.title: Red Sun Camels and Broome Camel Safaris
cultural_refs.description: Broome's two camel tour operators, distinguished by blanket colour (Red Sun Camels red, Broome Camel Safaris blue), run the beach's signature sunrise and sunset rides.

cultural_refs.title: Broome's dinosaur footprints
cultural_refs.description: Footprints in the rocks near Cable Beach, part of trackways running about 80 km along the coast, are marketed by the Broome Visitor Centre as 120 million years old; Wikipedia gives 130 million years for the footprints at the beach itself. The two figures do not agree.

recurring_events.name: Staircase to the Moon
recurring_events.description: A full moon rising over the exposed mudflats of Roebuck Bay creates the illusion of a staircase to the moon. The Broome Visitor Centre puts it at 2-3 days a month between March and October; an older tourism source describes it as 3 nights a month; the sheet cannot resolve the discrepancy.

recurring_events.name: Shinju Matsuri long table dinner
recurring_events.when_text: Held at Cable Beach as part of the Shinju Matsuri festival
recurring_events.description: Cable Beach is the site of major tourism events including the Shinju Matsuri long table dinner, per the Broome Visitor Centre.

businesses.name: Red Sun Camels
businesses.description: Camel tour operator running sunrise and sunset rides on Cable Beach, identified by red blankets; enforces a 90 kg individual weight limit as of 2026.
businesses.source: Broome Visitor Centre, Camel Rides page (2026)

businesses.name: Broome Camel Safaris
businesses.description: Camel tour operator running sunrise and sunset rides on Cable Beach, identified by blue blankets; enforces a 90 kg individual weight limit as of 2026.
businesses.source: Broome Visitor Centre, Camel Rides page (2026)

things_to_know.label: Vehicle ramp closed
things_to_know.note: Cable Beach's vehicle access ramp has been closed since 3 June 2025 for the Walmanyjun Cable Beach foreshore redevelopment (Stage 2) and will not reopen until mid/late 2026; during the works, north of the rocks and the camels are reached on foot via the surf club beach access point only.

things_to_know.label: Speed limit
things_to_know.note: Vehicles permitted on the beach near Gantheaume Point and north of the rocks are limited to 15 km/h.

things_to_know.label: Lifeguard patrols
things_to_know.note: Daily dry-season patrols run in front of the Broome Surf Life Saving Club, marked by red and yellow flags; patrols are scheduled to resume for the 2026 dry season on Good Friday, 3 April 2026.

access_note: Broome International Airport (BME) is about 3.2 km from Cable Beach in a straight line; no road distance or drive time for that route is available in current sourcing. The beach itself is about 4 km west of the Broome central business district. Vehicle access to north of the rocks is currently pedestrian-only, via the surf club access point, while the beach's ramp is closed for redevelopment until mid/late 2026.
